title: The Enemy
summary: Pearl S. Buck's story is set in Japan during the Second World War. Dr Sadao Hoki, a Japanese surgeon, finds a wounded American prisoner of war and must choose between his duty as a doctor and his duty as a patriotic citizen. The story shows humanity rising above narrow national prejudice.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Pearl S. Buck (1892–1973) was an American novelist who spent much of her early life in Asia. She won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938 and often wrote about the meeting of Eastern and Western cultures.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Sadao, trained in America, lives with his wife Hana in a house by the Japanese coast. A badly wounded American sailor is washed ashore. Although sheltering an enemy is a crime, Sadao operates and saves him. The servants leave in protest. Sadao informs the General, who promises to send assassins but forgets. Finally Sadao helps the man escape by boat.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
• Background: Sadao's father valued education and tradition and sent him to America to study surgery. There Sadao met Hana, but married her in Japan only after his father approved. He is kept at home during the war because he is perfecting a discovery to keep wounds clean, and because the old General may need an operation.
  • The prisoner arrives: One misty evening the couple see a man crawl out of the sea and collapse. He is a young white man with a bullet wound; his cap shows he belongs to the American navy. They consider throwing him back into the sea but cannot. They carry him into the house.
  • The servants' reaction: The old gardener and Yumi, the maid, refuse to help. Yumi will not wash a white man, so Hana does it herself. The servants believe their master should let the man die, and later they all leave.
  • The operation: Hana, who has never seen surgery, gives the anaesthetic though she feels sick. Sadao removes the bullet with great skill. During recovery the couple treat the prisoner correctly but coldly; Hana notices marks of torture on him.
  • The General: Sadao tells the General everything. The General, who trusts no other surgeon, will not have Sadao arrested. He promises to send private assassins to kill the man quietly and remove the body. Sadao waits three restless nights, but no one comes.
  • The escape: Sadao puts food, water, extra clothing and a flashlight in a boat and tells the young man to row to a small uninhabited island nearby and wait for a Korean fishing boat. He is to signal with the flashlight if supplies run out. No signal comes: the prisoner has got away.
  • The ending: The General admits he forgot his promise, being absorbed in his own illness, and asks Sadao to keep the matter secret. Sadao recalls the unpleasant white faces he met in America and wonders why he could not kill this man.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Humanity above nationalism: a doctor's first duty is to save life, whoever the patient is.
  • Conflict of duties: private conscience against public loyalty.
  • Racial prejudice: both Sadao and the servants carry prejudice; Sadao overcomes it in action.
  • The futility of war: war makes enemies of people who have no personal quarrel.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
Dr Sadao Hoki: a brilliant surgeon and scientist, dutiful son and loyal Japanese. He dislikes Americans, yet his professional ethics will not let a wounded man die. He is courageous and resourceful, and honest enough to report to the General, yet compassionate enough to arrange the escape.

Hana: a devoted, dignified and brave wife. She shares her husband's fears, overcomes her revulsion to nurse the prisoner, manages the house alone when the servants leave and supports Sadao throughout.

The General: self-centred and practical. He protects Sadao only because he needs him, and forgets a matter of national security because of his own pain. Through him the author criticises the selfishness of those in authority.

The servants: they represent conventional, unquestioning patriotism and superstition.

notes.heading: Title and message
notes.html: The title is ironic. The American is an 'enemy' only by the accident of war; to a healer he is a human being in need. The story asks who the real enemy is: a wounded young man, or the hatred and prejudice that war creates. Its message is that compassion and professional duty must rise above narrow boundaries.

keyTerms.definition: A member of the armed forces captured and held by the enemy during war.
A substance that makes a patient unable to feel pain during surgery.
A person hired to kill someone secretly.
An unfair opinion formed without knowledge or reason, often against a race or group.
A situation requiring a difficult choice between two courses of action.
The moral principles that guide a person's conduct in their profession.

mcqs.q: Why was Dr Sadao not sent abroad with the troops?
options: The General might need an operation and Sadao was working on a discovery
mcqs.explanation: He was indispensable both as a scientist and as the General's surgeon.

mcqs.q: How did Sadao and Hana know the man was an American?
options: From the lettering on his cap
mcqs.explanation: His battered cap showed he belonged to the US Navy.

mcqs.q: Who washed the wounded man when the maid refused?
mcqs.explanation: Yumi would not touch a white man, so Hana did it herself.

mcqs.q: What did the General promise to do about the prisoner?
mcqs.explanation: He offered to have the man killed quietly and the body removed.

mcqs.q: Why did the assassins never come?
mcqs.explanation: The General was preoccupied with his own suffering.

mcqs.q: How did Sadao finally get rid of the prisoner?
options: He handed him to the army
He helped him escape by boat to an island
He sent him to a hospital
mcqs.explanation: He gave him a stocked boat and directions to wait for a Korean fishing boat.

mcqs.q: The servants left the house because they
mcqs.explanation: They thought it disloyal and feared the consequences.

mcqs.q: The central theme of the story is
mcqs.explanation: Sadao's choice to save a life overrides hostility between nations.

questions.q: Why did Sadao and Hana hesitate to help the wounded man?
questions.answerHtml: He was an American, an enemy of Japan in wartime. Sheltering him could lead to their arrest as traitors, while handing him over meant his certain death. They were torn between fear of the law and their human feeling.

questions.q: What role did Hana play during the operation?
questions.answerHtml: Though she had never witnessed surgery and felt sick, Hana obeyed her husband bravely. She fetched towels and the anaesthetic, administered it as instructed and stayed by his side, showing courage and loyalty.

questions.q: Why did the General spare the American prisoner?
questions.answerHtml: He did not spare him out of kindness. He needed Sadao for his own operation, so he would not report him. He promised to send assassins but, absorbed in his own illness, simply forgot.

questions.q: Dr Sadao was torn between his duty as a doctor and his duty as a citizen. How did he resolve the conflict?
questions.answerHtml:
As a patriotic Japanese, Sadao knew he should hand the American to the police. As a surgeon, trained to save lives, he could not let a bleeding man die. He chose first to be a doctor: he carried the man home, operated with great skill and nursed him back to strength, even after the servants left and his reputation was at risk.

He did not forget his duty as a citizen. He informed the General frankly and agreed to the plan of assassination, leaving the matter to authority. For three nights he waited, tense and sleepless. When nothing happened, he realised he would have to act himself.

He then found a way that satisfied both conscience and safety. He gave the prisoner a boat, food, water and a flashlight, and showed him how to reach an island and wait for a fishing boat. The enemy left Japan, his family was safe, and no life was taken. Sadao's humanity triumphed without betraying his country in any harmful way.

questions.q: Hana is a model of courage and compassion. Discuss her character with reference to the story.
questions.answerHtml:
Hana is far more than a traditional, obedient wife. When the wounded American appears, she is frightened and shares her husband's prejudice, yet she cannot agree to throw him back into the sea. It is she who suggests carrying him inside.

She shows courage in action. When Yumi refuses to wash the man, Hana does it herself. During the operation she overcomes nausea to give the anaesthetic. As the prisoner recovers she feeds him, and she feels real pain on seeing the scars of torture on his body.

She also shows strength of character. When the servants leave, she does the housework and cares for the children without complaint. She worries about her husband's safety and reputation but never abandons him or the patient. Her dignity, self-control and quiet sympathy make her the emotional centre of the story and an equal partner in Sadao's humane decision.
